prompt:
Summarize the notice below for a customer who owns one of these kettles, in no more than 80 words.

Safety recall: Hearthwell 1.7-liter electric kettles

Hearthwell is recalling about 48,000 electric kettles, model KT-170, sold between March and October of last year in supermarkets and online. The model number is printed on the base of the kettle. Only kettles with batch codes from 2304 to 2311, printed next to the model number, are affected.

In these kettles, the switch that turns the kettle off when the water boils can fail. If that happens, the kettle keeps heating until the water has boiled away, which can damage the base and, in rare cases, cause a fire. We have received 23 reports of failed switches, including two small fires. Nobody has been injured.

If you own an affected kettle, stop using it immediately and unplug it. You do not need the receipt. Visit hearthwell.example/recall or call 0800 555 0199 to arrange a free collection, and you will receive either a replacement kettle of a newer model or a full refund, whichever you prefer. Collections usually take place within ten working days.

Kettles with other batch codes, and all other Hearthwell products, are not affected and are safe to use. We are sorry for the inconvenience.
answer: Hearthwell is recalling KT-170 kettles with batch codes 2304 to 2311 (printed on the base), sold from March to October last year. Their shut-off switch can fail, so the kettle may boil dry and, rarely, catch fire. If yours is affected, stop using it and unplug it. No receipt is needed: visit hearthwell.example/recall or call 0800 555 0199 for a free collection, then choose a newer replacement or a full refund. Other batches are safe.

prompt:
Summarize the passage below for an 8-year-old in three or four short sentences.

When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, she flies back to the hive and tells her sisters where it is, without saying a word. She does it by dancing.

The most famous of these movements is the waggle dance. On the wall of the honeycomb, the bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then loops back around and repeats the run, again and again. The direction of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly. A run straight up the comb means "fly toward the sun"; a run tilted to the right of straight up means "fly that much to the right of the sun." The length of the waggle tells them how far to go: the longer the bee waggles, the farther away the flowers are.

The other bees crowd around the dancer and follow her movements with their antennae. They also smell the flowers' scent on her body, which helps them recognize the right flowers when they arrive.

The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent years studying these dances and won a Nobel Prize in 1973 for his discoveries about how bees communicate.
answer: When a honeybee finds lots of flowers, she flies home and does a special dance to tell the other bees where they are. The direction she wiggles in shows which way to fly, compared with the sun. The longer she wiggles, the farther away the flowers are. The other bees also sniff the flower smell on her body, so they can find the right flowers.
